README.title: cdp-web
README.html:
cdp-web

A retro computing themed node-graph front-end for the Composers Desktop Project webassembly port (cdp-wasm).

Sounds are built on a modular desktop: each process is a small window you wire to others with patch cables, so you can audition a whole chain and tweak it as you listen.

How the patcher works

1. Add a process. Use the menus (or double-click the empty desktop to search) to drop a process onto the desktop. There are three families: sound effects, generators that make sound from nothing, and Faust devices you can program yourself. 2. Give it a sound. Drop an audio file from your computer anywhere on the desktop (it becomes a Source window), use a Source's Choose file… / URL… buttons, or start from a generator. Cables carry audio from one node's output ○ to the next node's input ○. 3. Set the controls. Each parameter has a slider and a plain-language description. Right-click a slider to type an exact value. Many parameters can also *change over time* — see Breakpoint envelopes. 4. Render and listen. Render the chain and play the result. Turn on Options ▸ Auto Render to re-render automatically as you make changes.

Finding your way around

  • Recipes — ready-made patches (File ▸ Recipes) that render a

sound the moment you open them; the quickest way to hear what CDP can do.

  • Effect reference — every sound-transforming process,

grouped by category, with its parameters explained.

  • Generators — synths and noise sources that create audio

from scratch.

  • Faust nodes — write your own DSP (or start from a preset) and

run it right in the graph.

  • Concepts guide — a few ideas that pay off across many

processes: time-varying parameters, spectral (phase-vocoder) effects, and how stereo is handled.

  • Saving & sharing — .cdp patch files, saving to a chosen

location, and sharing a whole patch as a link.

New to CDP? Check the concepts guide, then browse the effect reference and start patching.

data-programs.title: Data-producing programs (analysis & data-file tools)
data-programs.html:
Data-producing programs (analysis & data-file tools)

An inventory of bundled CDP programs whose useful output is data, not audio — pitch contours, onset/peak times, spectral peaks, feature lists, MIDI, and the breakpoint/pitch/column text files those feed. The typed effect catalog (EFFECTS / applyEffect) is audio-in → audio-out, so these programs are structurally invisible to it even though they're bundled and runnable via cdp.run(...). This is the same class the envelope helpers (extractEnvelope) already tap.

Every bundled program was surveyed and classed by I/O shape; this page lists the ANALYSIS and DATA classes (the untapped ones). Audio effects and generators are covered by the effect reference and generator reference.

Last surveyed: 2026-07-11 (CDP 7.1). Programs marked ✅ were run in WASM here; others are classified from CDP help + source and should be spot-checked before wrapping.

Analysis — sound → data

Extract information *from* a sound (or its spectral analysis). These are the high-value ones for a UI: they produce curves and markers to draw, edit, and reuse.

ProgramExtractsOutputNotes
pvoc anal ✅phase-vocoder spectral analysis.anaThe front end of every spectral chain; already used internally.
repitch getpitch ✅pitch contourbinary pitch → time freq textShipped as the getPitch helper (recovers a 220 Hz harmonic tone).
peakfind ✅amplitude-peak timestime list textfileShipped as the findPeaks helper; transient/slice detector, any channel count.
sndinfo ✅max sample, zero-crossings, holes, props, sample dumpstdout / textfileMulti-mode inspector (maxsamp, zcross, findhole, prntsnd, props).
onsetsound-onset times per channeltime list textfileMultichannel input only (errors on mono).
get_partialsrelative partial freqs + amplitudes of a pitched soundFRQ- or MIDI-and-amplitude textFrom a single analysis window (modes 1–2) or window at a time (3–4).
featuresprominent spectral features / peak datatext data files + statsModes cut/envelope features or report prominent-peak frequencies.
fturanal analsegment start-times, formant-median freqs, brightnesstext feature datasynth mode resynthesises from the data.
peak extractper-window spectral peaks or pitch-streamstime frq:amp text / filter-varibankFrom an analysis file.
specanalPVOC / FFT / cepstrum / formant / pitch / HF analysis.ana, text data, MIDI varibankA whole analysis toolbox in one program.
specavtime-averaged spectrumfrq amp textfileAverage spectrum of one or more sounds.
specinfospectral peaks / energy / octave-band datatext dataModes peak / report / print / octvu.
specvuone analysis window's data, or min/max frq & amptextfileSpectral snapshot for inspection.
spectune (4, 6)found pitch / median pitch per segmentreported valuesModes 4 & 6 report pitch and write no sound.
pitchinfoinfo on a binary pitch file; convert → breakpoint textstdout / time freq textsee/hear are audio/display; convert is the data path.
rmsinfoRMS / average / DC levelstdoutportsf external.
search sigstartearliest time signal appears across filesstdout

Data-file tools — data → data (and data generators)

Transform or synthesise the text/data files CDP effects consume — breakpoints, pitch data, columns, filter banks, mixfiles. The breakpoint half of this is what warpBreakpoints already exposes (envel replot).

ProgramDoesI/O
envel (replot/create/envtobrk/…) ✅the breakpoint envelope toolkitbrk/env ⇄ brk/env
ptobrk ✅binary pitch data → time freq breakpoint textpitch → brk
brktopitext pitch data → binary pitch filebrk → pitch
convert_to_midifreq-breakpoint + peak-level text → Standard MIDItext → .mid/.rmi
columns / getcol / putcolmanipulate / extract / insert columns of numberstext ⇄ text
smoothsmooth a frq amp spectral-data textfiletext → text
cubicsplinespline-smooth frq amp data into a curvetext → text
tsconvertrectify / quantise / log / to-breakpoint a numeric listtext → text/brk
vectorsmanipulate two columns of numbers (vectors)text → text/stdout
notchinvertinvert spectral notches in a frq amp textfiletext → text
peakisoisolate spectral peaks in a frq amp textfiletext → text
oneformextract single-moment formants from a formant datafile.for → text
vuformdump a formant file's spectral-envelope values.for → text
filtragegenerate randomised fixed / time-varying filter-bank data→ varibank text
refocusgenerate focus/level envelope breakpoint textfiles→ brk set
rmrespgenerate room early-reflection breakpoint data→ brk
spacedesigngenerate enveloping / mixing control files→ control files
dshiftpan-breakpoint → Doppler semitone-shift breakpointbrk → brk
hfpermharmony-field chord & delay permutation data→ MIDI/pitch text
unknot(un)knot rhythmic-pattern textfilestext → text
histconvCDP process-history log → readable textlog → text
analjoinconcatenate several analysis files.ana → .ana
multimix / panorama / transitbuild multichannel mixfiles for submix/newmixsounds → mixfile text

Audio → MIDI

A real pipeline exists: extract a pitch contour and peak levels, then convert.

  • repitch getpitch → ptobrk → time freq + peakfind/level data → convert_to_midi → .mid
  • get_partials (modes 2/4) emits MIDI-pitch + amplitude lists directly.
  • specanal writes a MIDI varibank; chirikov modes 3–4 emit a MIDI-pitch breakpoint.

The rest (for completeness, not untapped features)

  • Audio effects — the large majority; the catalog wraps 142 effects across

42 CDP programs (incl. newtex), the rest are catalog candidates.

  • Generators — 16 synthesis generators wrapped (incl. strands); others:

newscales, spectrum, ts (text/data-driven synthesis), pulser synth.

  • Multichannel / format tools (MCTOOL) — interlx, chorder, channelx,

chxformat, copysfx, njoin, nmix, mton, repair, frame, pairex, newmix, mchstereo, fmdcode, abfdcode, sfprops… (some wrapped as externals).

  • Display-only (out of scope) — pview, pagrab, paview, pdisplay,

gobosee, formants see/getsee: render to screen / SoundLoom / PostScript.

  • Utility / housekeeping — housekeep, sndinfo (stdout modes), maxsamp2,

stretcha, brkdur, diskspace, asciiget, listdate, logdate, progmach, tkusage, fixgobo, gobo, paudition, pmodify.

  • Interactive-usage crash (fixed) — fracture, iterfof, strands,

newtex (and newsynth) page their long usage text with a "PRESS ANY KEY" wait built on conio's kbhit/getch, which the WASM side modules didn't provide — so cdp help <prog> and any no-arg call trapped, though a correctly-argumented run was always fine. Weak kbhit/getch/getche stubs in scripts/cdp_core_stubs.c now satisfy the link, so usage prints and the programs run normally.

Helper surface

Mirroring the envelope helpers, a small analysis API lets apps get editable curves and markers without hand-writing argv (each is a thin cdp.run wrapper + a parser, covered by test/analysis.mjs).

Shipped (cdp-wasm):

HelperChainReturns
getPitch(cdp, wav) ✅pvoc anal → repitch getpitch[[t, Hz], …] (empty if unpitched)
findPeaks(cdp, wav, {windowMs, threshold}) ✅peakfind[t, …] peak times

Candidates (not yet built):

HelperChainReturns
findOnsets(cdp, wav, {level})onsetper-channel onset times (multichannel input)
getPartials(cdp, wav, {time})pvoc anal → get_partials[[Hz, amp], …]
audioToMidi(cdp, wav, …)pitch + levels → convert_to_midi.mid bytes

getPitch unlocks pitch-curve display, autotune targets and audio-to-MIDI in a consuming app; its chain already existed inside the catalog as derivePitch.

effects/README.title: Effect reference
effects/README.html:
Effect reference

232 effects across 110 CDP programs, grouped by category. Each links to its program page.

Combine

  • Spectral mean — combine.mean — Combine two sounds by taking the mean of their spectra (a hybrid).
  • Spectral cross — combine.cross — Replace the spectral amplitudes of the first sound with those of the second (cross-synthesis).
  • Spectral sum — combine.sum — Add the two spectra together.
  • Spectral difference — combine.diff — Subtract the second spectrum from the first (spectral cancellation).
  • Spectral interleave — combine.interleave — Interleave alternating blocks of analysis frames from the two sounds.
  • Spectral maximum — combine.max — Keep, in every channel and frame, the louder of the two spectra.
  • Convolve — modify.convolve — Convolve the first sound with the second (cross-filtering / impulse-response colouring).
  • Subtract signal — subtract.subtract — Sample-by-sample subtract the 2nd sound (mixed to mono) from one channel of the 1st — cancel shared material or take a difference.
  • Amplitude transplant — specsphinx.impose — Impose the channel amplitudes of the second sound onto the channel frequencies of the first.
  • Spectral multiply — specsphinx.multiply — Multiply the two spectra together — only frequencies present in both sounds survive.
  • Spectral denoise — speclean.clean — Remove noise from the first sound using the second as a noise profile (the second input should be a sample of noise or room tone alone).

Delay & reverb

  • Tuned delay — newdelay.newdelay — Short tuned delay producing a resonant pitch.
  • Delay / resonance — modify.revecho — Delay with feedback — short times give resonance, long times give echo.
  • Convolution reverb — fastconv.reverb — Convolve the sound with an impulse response (reverb IR or FIR filter) on the 2nd input.
  • Reverb — reverb.reverb — Algorithmic multichannel reverb (fills 1–8 output channels).
  • Room reverb — reverb.room — Room-model multichannel reverb with small/medium/large presets.
  • Echoes — sfecho.echo — Discrete, non-overlapping echoes of the whole sound, dying away.
  • Multichannel echoes — mchanrev.stadium — Scatter decaying "stadium" echoes of the source around a multichannel field.

Envelope

  • Tremolo — tremolo.tremolo — Amplitude modulation (tremolo).
  • Tremolo (envelope) — envel.tremolo — Impose a tremolo (amplitude) envelope on the sound.
  • Tremolo (narrowing) — tremenv.tremenv — Tremolo whose width narrows after each peak.
  • Swell — envel.swell — Fade in to and out from a peak moment (peak must be within the file).
  • Emphasise attack — envel.attack — Boost the loudest point as an attack transient.
  • Fade in/out (dovetail) — envel.dovetail — Dovetail the file by fading the start in and the end out.
  • Fade to silence — envel.curtail — Fade the sound to silence starting at a given time within it.
  • Amplitude ramp — envel.scaled — Impose a linear amplitude ramp across the whole sound (crescendo / decrescendo).
  • Level (equalise) — flatten.flatten — Even out the loudness of successive sound elements (levels the dynamics).
  • Spike envelope — spike.spike — Envelope the whole sound to swell to a single peak at a chosen time.
  • Exponential decay — envnu.expdecay — Impose an exponential fade-to-silence from a chosen start time.
  • Peak chop — envnu.peakchop — Isolate the attack peaks and replay them at a set tempo. Needs rhythmic input.

Extend & segment

  • Loop segment — extend.loop — Loop a segment from the start of the file a number of times.
  • Iterate (fluid) — extend.iterate — Iterate the whole sound in a fluid manner with random pitch/time scatter.
  • Doublets — extend.doublets — Cut the source into segments and repeat each one (stuttering).
  • Zigzag — extend.zigzag — Read back and forth (zigzag) inside the first part of the file.
  • Freeze / sustain — extend.freeze — Freeze a segment and re-sound it to fill a longer duration (granular sustain).
  • Drunk walk — extend.drunk — Splice segments read by a drunken walk around a moving point in the source.
  • Back-to-back — extend.baktobak — Abut the sound to a reversed copy of itself at the join point (palindrome).
  • Repeat at times — extend.repetitions — Replay the whole source at a series of evenly-spaced times (echo/overlay).
  • Bouncing repeat — repeater.bounce — Repeat a segment with accelerating, dimming bounces (like a dropped object settling).
  • Respeed events — retime.speed — Find silence-separated events and change their speed. Needs rhythmic/percussive input.
  • Tighten silences — constrict.constrict — Shorten (or close up) the silent gaps in a sound, tightening its rhythm.
  • Bounce — bounce.bounce — Bounce the whole sound: accelerating repeats that die away, like a dropped ball settling.
  • Splinter into — splinter.into — A stream of tiny, rising splinters of the sound leads into it at the chosen point.
  • Splinter away — splinter.outof — The sound plays to the chosen point, then shatters into a stream of shrinking splinters.
  • Shrinking repeats — shrink.shrink — Repeat the sound with each repeat shorter than the last, closing up as it goes.
  • Fast wind — dvdwind.dvdwind — Shorten the sound by keeping small clips and skipping between them (fast-wind scan).
  • Segment zigzag — distmore.segszig — Zigzag back and forth across the sound with progressively shrinking sweeps.
  • Cascade echoes — cascade.cascade — Echo successive segments of the source and superimpose the echo-sets.
  • Fractalise — frfractal.fractal — Build a self-similar (fractal) expansion of the sound.
  • FOF iterate (pitch line) — iterfof.line — Re-sound the source as a rapid stream of short packets at a chosen pitch (FOF-style vocal synthesis), with vibrato and random scatter.
  • Repeat syllables — envspeak.repeat — Detect speech-like syllables and repeat each one (stutter). Needs articulated, speech-like input.
  • Shuffle syllables — envspeak.shuffle — Detect speech-like syllables and reorder them at random (repeatable per seed). Needs articulated input.
  • Stutter — stutter.stutter — Slice the source into elements and replay randomly cut segments of them in random order, with optional silences (speech-stutter effect).
  • Iterate on a pitch line — iterline.iterline — Re-sound the source repeatedly while its transposition follows a line from a start to an end pitch.
  • Shifting cycles — shifter.cycles — Layer the sound into simultaneous repeating cycles of different lengths, moving a louder “focus” from one to the next.
  • Partition (wavesets) — partition.wavesets — Deal a mono sound out across several files in waveset-sized blocks (silence fills the gaps).
  • Partition (time blocks) — partition.blocks — Deal a mono sound out across several files in fixed-length time blocks.
  • Cut to enveloped grains — distcut.envelope — Chop a mono sound into a sequence of separate waveset-grains, each with a falling envelope.
  • Cut to enveloped slices — envcut.envelope — Chop a mono sound into a sequence of separate fixed-length slices, each with a falling envelope.
  • Cantor holes (proportional) — cantor.holes — Cantor-set erosion: cut a hole in the middle third, then in the pieces that remain, and so on — output is the growing sequence.
  • Cantor holes (fixed) — cantor.holesfixed — Cantor-set erosion with fixed-length holes: the growing sequence of ever-more-perforated sounds.
  • Cantor vibrato layers — cantor.vibrato — Cantor-set erosion driven by superimposed vibrato envelopes — a shimmering sequence of perforated sounds.
  • Isolate loud segments — isolate.threshold — Extract the loud events from a mono sound into one file (they keep their original timing), plus a remnant file of the leftovers.
  • Slice into pieces — isolate.slices — Cut a mono sound into equal-length pieces, each written to its own file.
  • Rejoin segments — rejoin.rejoin — Remix segment files from Partition / Isolate back into one sound (the inverse operation). Supply the segments as extra.inputs.

Filter & dynamics

  • Low-pass filter — filter.lohi — Fixed low-pass: frequencies above the stop band are removed.
  • Noise gate — gate.gate — Replace sound below the threshold with silence.
  • Gate (remove gaps) — gate.edit — Edit out (delete) the stretches quieter than the threshold, shortening the sound.
  • Clip — clip.clip — Hard-clip the signal at the given level (distortion).
  • Clip half-waves — clip.half — Clip each half-waveform at a fraction of its own peak (level-following distortion).
  • Boost/cut band — filter.fixed — Boost or cut a band of frequencies centred on a frequency.
  • Sweeping band-pass — filter.sweeping — Band-pass filter whose focus frequency sweeps up and down a range.
  • Resonant band-pass — filter.bandpass — Resonant band-pass: passes a band around the centre frequency, the rest attenuated.
  • Resonant notch — filter.notch — Resonant notch (band-reject): removes a band around the centre frequency.
  • Resonant low-pass — filter.resonlo — Resonant low-pass with an emphasised cutoff (synth-style).
  • Resonant high-pass — filter.resonhi — Resonant high-pass with an emphasised cutoff (synth-style).
  • Phaser — filter.phasing — Classic phasing effect (mix of signal with a phase-shifted copy).
  • Shudder — modify.shudder — Shudder a stereo sound with scattered amplitude dips of random depth and width.
  • Iterated filter bank — filter.iterated — Iterate the sound, cumulatively filtering each repeat through a tuned filter bank.
  • Harmonic filter bank — filter.bank — A bank of resonant filters tuned to a harmonic series over the root frequency.

Formants

  • Vocoder (cross-synth) — formants.vocode — Impose the spectral envelope (formants) of the second sound onto the first.
  • Envelope transfer — specenv.replace — Replace the spectral envelope of the first sound with that of the second (the second sound must be at least as long as the first).
  • Spectral twin — spectwin.hybrid — Build a hybrid of the two sounds by exchanging their spectral frequencies and envelopes.

Granular

  • Hover (zigzag read) — hover.hover — Hover over a point in the file, zigzag-reading it at a frequency.
  • Duplicate grains — grain.duplicate — Repeat each detected grain N times. Needs rhythmic/percussive input.
  • Grain time-warp — grain.timewarp — Stretch the time between grains without stretching the grains. Needs rhythmic input.
  • Reverse grain order — grain.reverse — Reverse the order of grains without reversing the grains. Needs rhythmic input.
  • Granular pitch-shift — modify.brassage — Granular reconstitution that pitch-shifts the source (transposition ratio).
  • Omit grains — grain.omit — Keep K out of every N detected grains (rhythmic thinning). Needs rhythmic input.
  • Reorder grains — grain.reorder — Reorder grains following a fixed jump pattern. Needs rhythmic input.
  • Align grains (2 sounds) — grain.align — Retime the grains of the second sound onto the grain-onset times of the first.
  • Repitch grains — grain.repitch — Transpose each detected grain by a number of semitones. Needs rhythmic input.
  • Wrappage (spatial brassage) — wrappage.wrappage — Granulate the source and scatter the grains over a multichannel field, with time-stretch or freeze and pitch shift.
  • Hover 2 (symmetric zigzag) — hover2.hover2 — Hover over a point in the file, zigzag-reading it into symmetrical zero-centred waveforms.
  • Extend grain region — grainex.extend — Find grains in a region of the sound and extend it by repeating them. Needs rhythmic/grainy input.

Mix

  • Mix two sounds — submix.merge — Mix the first and second sounds together (mono or stereo), with optional offset and balance.
  • Split channels — housekeep.split — Split a sound into its channels, one mono file each (left first) — a bank of sounds.
  • Join channels (interleave) — submix.interleave — Interleave two (mono) sounds into one stereo file: first → left, second → right. The inverse of Split channels.

Morph

  • Spectral morph — morph.morph — Interpolate (morph) from the first sound into the second over a span of time.
  • Spectral bridge — morph.bridge — Interpolate across the whole sound between the two spectra (a bridge from one to the other).
  • Peak morph — newmorph.morph — Morph between dissimilar spectra by moving the spectral peaks of the first sound onto those of the second.
  • Tune to harmonic field — newmorph.tune — Gradually tune the first sound to the (averaged) harmonic field of the second.
  • Partial cross — specross.partials — Interpolate the partials of one pitched sound towards those of another (both sounds must be clearly pitched).

Pitch & time

  • Transpose (speed) — modify.speed — Vary speed and pitch together by a number of semitones.
  • Gain — modify.loudness — Scale the loudness of the sound.
  • Time stretch — stretch.time — Phase-vocoder time-stretch without changing pitch.
  • Stack (harmoniser) — modify.stack — Stack transposed copies of the source on the original (octave/chord doubler).
  • Time stretch (smooth) — spectstr.stretch — Phase-vocoder time-stretch that breaks up channel coherence to suppress the usual stretch artefacts.
  • Accelerando — strans.accel — Accelerate (or decelerate) smoothly towards a goal speed, tape-style (pitch follows).
  • Vibrato — strans.vibrato — Add vibrato: wobble the pitch of the sound at a set rate and depth.
  • Verge glisses — verges.verges — Play the source with brief pitch-gliss "verges" swooping onto chosen moments.
  • Fractal wave — fractal.wave — Recursively transpose the sound over a self-similar pitch pattern — a fractal cascade of speed-ups and slow-downs.

Pitch-data

  • Quantise pitch (autotune) — repitch.quantise — Snap the detected pitch to a major scale (autotune), preserving formants. Needs a pitched, monophonic source.
  • Smooth pitch (de-vibrato) — repitch.smooth — Smooth the detected pitch contour over a time window (removes vibrato/jitter). Needs a pitched source.
  • Invert pitch contour — repitch.invert — Mirror the detected pitch contour around a pivot pitch (melodic inversion). Needs a pitched source.

Pitch-sync grains

  • Pitch-sync stretch — psow.stretch — Time-stretch by repositioning pitch-synchronous grains. Pitch is auto-detected; the hint is used if none is found.
  • Pitch-sync duplicate — psow.dupl — Lengthen by duplicating pitch-synchronous grains. Pitch is auto-detected; the hint is used if none is found.
  • Freeze grain (sustain) — psow.sustain — Freeze and sustain a single grain into a held tone, with optional vibrato.
  • Tweets — tweet.tweet — Replace the voiced pulses of the sound with synthetic birdsong-like tweets. Pitch is auto-detected; the hint is used if none is found.
  • Pulses to noise — tweet.noise — Replace the voiced pulses of the sound with bursts of noise (whispered/breathy version of the source).

Spatialisation

  • Pan (mono → stereo) — modify.space — Place a (mono-mixed) source at a position in the stereo field.
  • Spin stereo image — spin.stereo — Spin a (stereo) image around the stereo field, with optional doppler.
  • B-format pan — abfpan.bformat — Pan a mono source into 1st-order B-format (4-channel ambisonic W/X/Y/Z), optionally rotating.
  • Multichannel spread — mchanpan.spread — Spread a mono source outward from a centre channel across a multichannel field.
  • Phasing (multi-stream) — phasor.phasor — Classic phasing from several phase-shifted copies of a mono source, spread across the output channels.
  • Shred to multichannel — mchshred.shred — Cut the sound into random chunks and reassemble them in random order, spraying the segments across a multichannel field.
  • Spatial syncopation — madrid.syncopate — Repeat the source as a pulse in spatially separated streams, randomly deleting repeats to syncopate the rhythm around the space.
  • Stereo enhance — phase.stereo — Widen a stereo image by phase-cancelling each channel out of the other.
  • Resync cycles — ceracu.cycles — Repeat the source in phasing cyclestreams that drift apart and resynchronise across the output channels (Reich-style phase loops).
  • Fracture (fragment scatter) — fracture.fracture — Shatter the source into enveloped fragments dealt out across the channels in pulsing waves.
  • Tesselate (phase pattern) — tesselate.tesselate — Steve-Reich-style phase pattern: the source repeats across channel pairs whose delays drift apart and resynchronise.
  • Flutter (spatial tremolo) — flutter.flutter — Bounce a loudness tremor between the left and right channels, fluttering the sound around the stereo field.
  • Spread to channels — multimix.spread — Place each input sound on its own output channel (N mono sounds → an N-channel file). Supply the extra sounds as extra.inputs.
  • Distribute across N channels — multimix.channels — Deal the input sounds, in order, across a fixed number of output channels. Supply the extra sounds as extra.inputs.
  • Spatial panorama — panorama.spatial — Distribute several mono sounds around a ring of loudspeakers, spread from left to right. Supply the extra sounds as extra.inputs.
  • Crumble to 8 channels — crumble.crumble — Project a mono sound onto an 8-channel ring, then progressively crumble it into segments scattered over smaller and smaller channel groups.
  • Crumble to 16 channels — crumble.crumble16 — Like Crumble, but onto a 16-channel ring split down to eight images.
  • Tangent motion (8ch) — tangent.tangent — Play repetitions of a mono sound along a tangent path to or from an 8-channel loudspeaker ring.
  • Transit motion (8ch) — transit.transit — Send repetitions of a mono sound crossing an 8-channel loudspeaker ring along a chosen path.

Spectral

  • Spectral blur — blur.blur — Time-average the spectrum over N analysis windows.
  • Spectral average — blur.avrg — Average each spectral band with its frequency neighbours.
  • Suppress partials — blur.suppress — Remove the N loudest partials in each window.
  • Trace partials — hilite.trace — Retain only the N loudest partials (spectral thinning).
  • Exaggerate contour — focus.exag — Exaggerate the spectral contour (sharpen peaks).
  • Spectral stretch — stretch.spectrum — Stretch the frequencies of the spectrum above the divide point.
  • Spectral chorus — blur.chorus — Chorus by randomising partial amplitudes and frequencies.
  • Drunk walk — blur.drunk — Read the spectrum by a random (drunken) walk over analysis windows.
  • Shuffle windows — blur.shuffle — Shuffle the order of spectral analysis windows by a domain→image pattern.
  • Spectral noise — blur.noise — Inject noise into the spectrum (0 = none, 1 = saturated).
  • Spectral scatter — blur.scatter — Randomly thin the spectrum, keeping N blocks per window.
  • Spread peaks — blur.spread — Spread the spectral peaks, introducing controlled noisiness.
  • Weave windows — blur.weave — Read the spectrum by weaving forward and back through the analysis windows.
  • Blur + trace — hilite.bltr — Time-average the spectrum and then retain only the N loudest partials.
  • Spectral low-pass — hilite.splow — Low-pass the spectrum (frequency-domain).
  • Spectral high-pass — hilite.sphigh — High-pass the spectrum (frequency-domain).
  • Spectral band-pass — hilite.spband — Band-pass the spectrum between two frequencies (frequency-domain).
  • Spectral notch — hilite.spnotch — Reject a band of the spectrum between two frequencies (frequency-domain notch).
  • Emphasise changes — hilite.pluck — Emphasise moments of spectral change (plucked/transient-like).
  • Arpeggiate spectrum — hilite.arpeg — Sweep a boosted band up and down the spectrum, arpeggiating its partials.
  • Split-band gain — hilite.band — Split the spectrum at a frequency and scale the low and high bands independently.
  • Fold into range — focus.fold — Octave-transpose all spectral components into a chosen frequency band.
  • Step-freeze — focus.step — Freeze the spectrum at regular time intervals (stepped, stuttering texture).
  • Accumulate — focus.accu — Sustain each spectral band until louder energy arrives, building an accumulating wash.
  • Focus on peaks — focus.focus — Concentrate spectral energy onto the strongest peaks (pitch/formant focusing).
  • Hold spectrum — focus.hold — Freeze the spectrum at a chosen moment and sustain it, stretching the sound.
  • Freeze spectrum — focus.freeze — Freeze the spectral character of the sound from a given moment onward.
  • Glisten (partition) — glisten.glisten — Randomly partition the spectrum into sets and play them back in turn.
  • Frequency shift — strange.shift — Slide the whole spectrum by a fixed number of Hz (linear shift → inharmonic/bell-like).
  • Waver (in/harmonic) — strange.waver — Oscillate between the harmonic sound and a spectrally-stretched inharmonic version.
  • Spectral invert — strange.invert — Invert the spectrum, turning spectral peaks into troughs (timbral negative).
  • Spectral glissando — strange.glis — Create an endless Shepard-tone glissando inside the source’s spectral envelope.
  • Super accumulate — superaccu.superaccu — Sustain every spectral band until louder sound arrives there, building a long, ringing resonant wash.
  • Narrow formants — specfnu.narrow — Steepen the formant peaks of the spectrum, sharpening the vowel-like resonances. Needs a pitched source.
  • Invert formants — specfnu.vibrate — Turn formant peaks into troughs and troughs into peaks, optionally cycling between original and inverted.
  • Spectral fold — specfold.fold — Fold a group of spectral channels over on itself, crossing frequency data.
  • Scramble spectral channels — specfold.randomise — Randomly permute a group of spectral channels, scattering frequency data.
  • Randomise window order — specnu.rand — Shuffle the time-order of the analysis windows, scrambling the sound’s evolution.
  • Spectral squeeze — specnu.squeeze — Compress the whole spectrum in frequency around a centre, narrowing its range.
  • Remove a pitch — specnu.remove — Find a pitch in the spectrum and strip it and its harmonics away.
  • Self-similarity — selfsim.selfsim — Replace spectral windows with the louder windows they most resemble, making the sound more self-similar.
  • Swap FFT real/imag — matrix.swap — Exchange the real and imaginary parts of the sound’s FFT — a metallic, phase-mangled glitch.
  • Invert FFT phase — matrix.invphase — Flip the phase of every FFT channel, subtly (or not so subtly) recolouring the sound.
  • Suppress partials — suppress.partials — Remove the N loudest spectral components in a band, leaving the residual noise and halo around them.

Spectral pitch

  • Transpose spectrum — repitch.transpose — Transpose the spectrum (the spectral envelope moves with it).
  • Transpose part of spectrum — pitch.transp — Transpose only the part of the spectrum above a split frequency.
  • Pick harmonics — pitch.pick — Keep only the spectral channels near the harmonics of a fundamental (pitch sieve).
  • Tune to pitch — pitch.tune — Replace the spectral frequencies with harmonics of a target pitch (spectral retuning).
  • Spectral chord — pitch.chord — Superimpose transposed copies of the spectrum on the original, building a chord.
  • Octave up (keep formants) — pitch.octmove — Transpose up by an octave (or harmonic ratio) without shifting the formants. Needs a pitched source.
  • Octave down (keep formants) — pitch.octmovedn — Transpose down by an octave (or harmonic ratio) without shifting the formants. Needs a pitched source.
  • Delete alternate harmonics — pitch.altharms — Delete the odd harmonics — an octave-up transposition with no formant change (hollow, clarinet-like). Needs a pitched source.
  • Auto-tune (nearest note) — spectune.nearest — Find the most prominent pitch in the sound and transpose it to the nearest tempered (keyboard) note.
  • Transpose (keep formants) — specfnu.transpose — Transpose the pitch while keeping the formant envelope in place (voice keeps its character).
  • Tune to chord — tunevary.chord — Pull the spectrum onto the harmonics of a chosen chord (spectral retuning to several pitches at once).

Synthesis

  • Make wavetable — waveform.make — Extract a short segment and mirror it into a symmetric wavecycle — a wavetable cut from the sound.
  • Wavetable (half-wavesets) — waveform.halfwaves — Build a wavetable from a group of half-wavesets at a point in the sound.
  • Wavetable + sine — waveform.sinemix — Make a wavetable by crossing a sound segment with a sine wave.
  • Sound packet — packet.make — Isolate/shape one enveloped sound packet (a short grain) from the source.

Texture

  • Texture (event cloud) — texture.simple — Scatter copies of the source into a cloud of events at random times and pitches.
  • Grain texture (spatial) — newtex.drunk — Scatter grains read as drunken walks through the source across a multichannel field.
  • Pulse stream — pulser.pulses — Chop the source into short enveloped packets and fire them out as a stream of pulses.
  • Pitched pulses — pulser.pitched — A stream of pitched packets: brightness comes from the source, the pitch from the MIDI pitch control.
  • Motor (pulse engine) — motor.motor — Machine-like texture: a fast inner pulse-stream cut from the source, driven under a slower rising-and-falling outer envelope.
  • Brownian texture — brownian.motion — Scatter transposed copies of the source into a stream that drifts through pitch and space by brownian motion.
  • Rotor (note-set cycles) — rotor.rotor — Spin the source into note-sets that grow and shrink in pitch-range, speed and stereo width as two cycles drift in and out of phase.
  • Crystal (rotating vertices) — crystal.rotate — Rotate a crystal of vertices in 3-D; each vertex fires an event whose stereo position, pitch and brightness trace the rotation.

Waveset distortion

  • Waveset multiply — distort.multiply — Repeat each waveset N times (raises pitch, adds grit).
  • Waveset average — distort.average — Average groups of wavesets together.
  • Waveset reverse — distort.reverse — Reverse wavesets in groups.
  • Waveset interpolate — distort.interpolate — Interpolate between successive wavesets (stretches & smears).
  • Waveset telescope — distort.telescope — Telescope (compress) groups of wavesets into one.
  • Waveset divide — distort.divide — Divide each wavecycle, adding subharmonics.
  • Waveset delete — distort.delete — Time-contract by keeping only 1 in every N wave-cycles.
  • Waveset replace — distort.replace — In each group of N wave-cycles, the strongest replaces the rest.
  • Waveset band-filter — distort.cyclefilter — Drop wave-cycles outside a pseudo-frequency band (waveset band-pass).
  • Waveset pitchwarp — distort.pitch — Randomly pitch-warp each wave-cycle (warbly, granular detuning).
  • Half-cycle shift — distshift.1 — Shift alternate groups of half-wavecycles forward in time.
  • Half-cycle swap — distshift.swap — Swap alternate groups of half-wavecycles.
  • Waveset scramble — scramble.scramble — Randomly reorder wavesets from the source.
  • Waveset omit — distort.omit — Silence A out of every B wavesets (gappy, rhythmic thinning).
  • Waveset repeat — distort.repeat — Repeat each wavecycle N times without time-stretching (roughens, lowers pitch).
  • Waveset overload — distort.overload — Clip the signal and overlay a noise distortion pattern on the clipped parts.
  • Waveset reform — distort.reform — Exaggerate the contour of each wavecycle (sharper, brighter).
  • Waveset fractal — distort.fractal — Superimpose miniature copies of each wavecycle onto itself (fractal graininess).
  • Waveset envelope — distort.envel — Impose a rising amplitude envelope over each group of N wavecycles (rhythmic pulsing).
  • Harmonic distortion — distort.harmonic — Superimpose chosen harmonics onto each wavecycle (adds richness/grit).
  • Waveset elongate — distort.elongate — Repeat each wavecycle N times, stretching the sound in time and lowering its pitch.
  • Power distort — quirk.power — Raise the waveform to a power — below 1 adds grit, above 1 smooths.
  • Wavecycle repeat-stretch — distrep.stretch — Time-stretch by repeating each wave-cycle group (with splices).
  • Waveset group-repeat — distortt.repeat — Repeat groups of wavesets until the requested duration is filled.
  • Waveset octave-up — distmore.double — Double (or quadruple…) the frequency of each waveset — octave shifts up.
  • Waveset interpolate (marks) — distmark.interp — Rebuild the sound by interpolating between waveset-groups found at marked times (glassy waveset morphing).

See also the generator reference and the conceptual guide.

effects/blur.title: blur
effects/blur.html:
blur

Spectral blurring — averaging and smearing phase-vocoder data over time and frequency.

Exposed effects: Spectral blur · Spectral average · Suppress partials · Spectral chorus · Drunk walk · Shuffle windows · Spectral noise · Spectral scatter · Spread peaks · Weave windows

Spectral blur

blur.blur · Spectral

Time-average the spectrum over N analysis windows.
  • Spectral — run through a pvoc anal → … → pvoc synth chain automatically; output is mono.

Parameters

ParamMeaningRangeDefaultTime-varying
windowsWindows1 – 10010yes

What it does

BLUR BLUR time-averages the spectrum. It 'blurs' detail in the time dimension by interpolating between the spectral envelope values of the start and end windows blurring windows. Note that it is not interpolating continuously over all the windows inbetween, just between the data in the start and end windows. The overall result is somewhat affected by just how different the data is in these two windows. The interpolation process produces a 'straight line' (linear) scale of values between the start and end points.

BLUR BLUR differs from HILITE BLTR in the absence of the 'trace' parameter. This means that the blurring occurs without any reduction in the number of partials.

Musical applications

As with all of these programs, the result is greatly affected by the nature of the input sound. The more windows blurred, the more blurring or smoothing of the sound you might expect to happen. However, you might not notice much difference if the sound is already constant (or similar at the start and end points). You will probably need a sound with a great deal of internal change for the blurring to have a perceptible effect.

The musical results of this process begin with a softening of the attack transients, so is highly effective with, for example, plucked or percussive sounds. A time-varying transition from the original to a very blurred effect can be achieved by a simple breakpoint file which sets a low value for blurring at the beginning of the sound and a high value at the end. It is possible for the sound to disappear gradually into its own ambience. This powerful technique can therefore useful in the creation of 'ambient' music, as well as any degree of softening of the original sound.

(…see the CDP source for the full discussion.)

Spectral average

blur.avrg · Spectral

Average each spectral band with its frequency neighbours.
  • Spectral — run through a pvoc anal → … → pvoc synth chain automatically; output is mono.

Parameters

ParamMeaningRangeDefaultTime-varying
neighboursNeighbours2 – 504yes

What it does

The averaging of energy information causes high energy data to cross channels. The result is the intrusion of timbral data into channels which previously didn't have that data. Test results led to a 'roughening' of the sound, though without going as far as distorting it.

Note that this process relates to channels, not to windows (as does the BLUR BLUR process). This means that the averaging directly affects the frequency components of the sound.

(…see the CDP source for the full discussion.)

Musical applications

BLUR AVRG appears to be useful to enrich the timbre of a sound and make its texture rougher.

Suppress partials

blur.suppress · Spectral

Remove the N loudest partials in each window.
  • Spectral — run through a pvoc anal → … → pvoc synth chain automatically; output is mono.

Parameters

ParamMeaningRangeDefaultTime-varying
partialsSuppress N loudest1 – 303yes

What it does

This process is the opposite of HILITE TRACE, which retains the N loudest partials. Whereas with TRACE many components have to be removed before the sound starts to be seriously affected, here the change to infile will be more immediate when a relatively small value for N is used.

Musical applications

The loudest partials will not necessarily relate to either the higher or lower parts of the frequency spectrum. They will relate simply to whatever is most audible ­ prominent ­ in the sound, such as possibly the fundamental of a pitched sound. This will have the effect of revealing the more strictly timbral aspects of the sound.

This process can also be useful in preparing a sound for another process which will benefit from suppressing its more audible features. As an example of this,... (I did a sound in which I couldn't get rid of the fundamental, which was reinforced by the process, when I really wanted to bring out other things.)

(…see the CDP source for the full discussion.)

Spectral chorus

blur.chorus · Spectral

Chorus by randomising partial amplitudes and frequencies.
  • Spectral — run through a pvoc anal → … → pvoc synth chain automatically; output is mono.

Parameters

ParamMeaningRangeDefaultTime-varying
aspreadAmp scatter1 – 1028200yes
fspreadFreq scatter1 – 42yes

What it does

Formerly SPECHORU, this process attempts to achieve a chorusing effect by randomising the amplitude and frequency values of the partials. It is based on an idea of Stephen McAdams. See his Spectral Fusion and the Creation of Auditory Images (1981).

If very large amplitude aspread values are used, the sound will turn to noise. The ranges shown for aspread and fspread appear to be rather extreme, but they are rescaled within the program. There is in fact no mathematical limit to the values which can be entered. In practice, the 'chorusing' effect itself is achieved by values just a little above 1!. Values of 2 or 3 begin to create a granular effect, and values of 10, 100 and 1000, for example, create more and more noise.

Musical applications

'Chorusing' is one of the standard effects used to enliven and enrich a sound. It becomes available here in an open-ended context, where the effect can be driven beyond the usual bounds into granulation and noise effects, useful when a certain textural or gritty quality is needed.

In Mode 5, a burbly but comprehensible vocal transformation may occur with aspread = 30 and fspread = 4.

Drunk walk

blur.drunk · Spectral

Read the spectrum by a random (drunken) walk over analysis windows.
  • Spectral — run through a pvoc anal → … → pvoc synth chain automatically; output is mono.

Parameters

ParamMeaningRangeDefaultTime-varying
rangeStep range1 – 505—
durDuration (s)0.5 – 82—

What it does

Beginning at starttime, a user-defined point in the infile, BLUR DRUNK moves through the file reading windows, but jumping either forwards or backwards, from one window to another, in a random way. The size of these random jumps cannot be greater than range. This random process is known as a drunken walk. It proceeds until the specified duration of the output sound has been generated.

If the process tries to leap right out of the soundfile at its end or its start, it is automatically reflected back into the sound near to the leap point. The process never reads backwards through the file, though it may leap backwards before starting its next read.

Musical applications

This process can be used to lurch about in a soundfile, producing a jumbled version of infile to varying degrees. The salient parameter is range. If range is small, the output will tend to linger around your start-point in the file, progressing very slowly away from it in an arbitrary direction. This results in a mix of time-stretching and slow wandering through the source. If range is large, the drunken walk tends to leap about wildly in the file, scrambling the source sound.

Shuffle windows

blur.shuffle · Spectral

Shuffle the order of spectral analysis windows by a domain→image pattern.
  • Spectral — run through a pvoc anal → … → pvoc synth chain automatically; output is mono.

Parameters

ParamMeaningRangeDefaultTime-varying
grpsizeGroup size1 – 201—

What it does

SHUFFLE shuffles windows in a PVOC analysis data file. This is a spectral version of 'brassage' (see MODIFY BRASSAGE and MODIFY SAUSAGE). As with most of these programs, the degree of audible difference is going to depend on how much the sound changes in the first place. Shuffling spectral windows in a fairly uniform sound may not have much effect. Experimenting with this program ought to lead to the unexpected.

To illustrate how this works, suppose there is a domain of three letters: A B C. This means that there will be three consecutive windows, numbered 1 2 3 in the order in which they occur in the analysis file.

(…see the CDP source for the full discussion.)

Musical applications

The domain-image parameter is what makes SHUFFLE particularly useful. The domain identifies a series of consecutive windows, and the image defines the order of those windows (some may be omitted). Then this whole pattern repeats as a block, affecting each consecutive set of windows in the source file. The control over re-ordering makes it possible to jumble, retrograde, mix forwards and backwards etc. the successive windows. An increasing grpsize makes more of the source audible at any given time, which means that one can play with the degree to which the source can be identified.

Thus one is stepping through the source in chunks of varying size and re-ordering the contents of those chunks. The re-orderings play with familiarity, create repeatable sub-patterns, and will lead to additional timbral changes depending on the degree to which differing spectral data get mixed together.

Spectral noise

blur.noise · Spectral

Inject noise into the spectrum (0 = none, 1 = saturated).
  • Spectral — run through a pvoc anal → … → pvoc synth chain automatically; output is mono.

Parameters

ParamMeaningRangeDefaultTime-varying
noiseNoise0 – 10.5yes

What it does

This functions enables one to move a sound source towards pure noise, by making the data in every channel – most of which is actually low level noise - equally loud. Total saturation will reduce all sounds to a very similar noise signal. Partial or gradual saturation is possible, through the use of values less than 1 or by using a time-varying breakpoint file. These work in the usual way, with gradual change between different time points to which are assigned different noise values.

Musical applications

This technique can be used to cause sound material to emerge from obscurity to clarity, or v.vs.. Also, a carefully chosen noise factor can be used to colour a sound or soften its edges.

Spectral scatter

blur.scatter · Spectral

Randomly thin the spectrum, keeping N blocks per window.
  • Spectral — run through a pvoc anal → … → pvoc synth chain automatically; output is mono.

Parameters

ParamMeaningRangeDefaultTime-varying
keepBlocks kept1 – 324yes

What it does

This function throws away a specified proportion of the analysis data in each window. Unlike HILITE TRACE, the channels chosen to be suppressed are selected entirely at random. The spectrum is thus thinned out in an unpredictable fashion.

Remember that the number of channels in an analysis file is determined by the value for the -N flag of the Phase Vocoder (now referred to as -c points). For example, if it was -c 1024, there will be 512 + 1 channels, each containing frequency and amplitude data.

(…see the CDP source for the full discussion.)

Musical applications

The musical result will be more variable than HILITE TRACE. The latter retains the N loudest channels, thus always keeping the most audibly prominent data of the original sound. BLUR SCATTER may or may not pick up audibly prominent data as it makes its random selections. The original sound material will therefore be more variably retained or cast aside, and this variability can be increased by using a time keep and/or a time blocksize breakpoint file.

SEE ALSO: TRACE, BLUR SUPPRESS, SUPPRESS (band)

Spread peaks

blur.spread · Spectral

Spread the spectral peaks, introducing controlled noisiness.
  • Spectral — run through a pvoc anal → … → pvoc synth chain automatically; output is mono.

Parameters

ParamMeaningRangeDefaultTime-varying
spreadSpread0 – 11yes

What it does

This process introduces noise into the spectrum in a way which is coherent with (i.e., related to) the spectral envelope. The spectral envelope (formants) in each window is retained, and the level in every channel is made to approximate this average spectral contour to a greater or lesser extent, depending on spread. This process tends to exaggerate the less prominent (noise) constituents of the spectrum.

Musical applications

This is a distortion technique which can be handled in a very sensitive manner because spread can be so finely adjusted, or altered in a time-varying manner. If applied to speech, the noise introduces a certain edginess, so if an effect such as unvoiced speech is sought, FORMANTS VOCODE is recommended, which allows some low or high frequency filtering.

Weave windows

blur.weave · Spectral

Read the spectrum by weaving forward and back through the analysis windows.
  • Spectral — run through a pvoc anal → … → pvoc synth chain automatically; output is mono.

Parameters

ParamMeaningRangeDefaultTime-varying
fwdForward step2 – 203—
backBack step0 – 192—

What it does

BLUR WEAVE is similar to SHUFFLE but is a smoother process which plots a regular course through the analysis windows, weaving backwards and forwards as instructed by the weavfile. Note that the weave process enables one to jump to points forwards or backwards in the soundfile, at which point it takes a single window. Thus one of the keys to understanding WEAVE is to realise that it only takes one window at a time after it has moved somewhere. It doesn't fill in with the windows inbetween. The weavfile therefore creates a sequence of single windows taken from various points relative to the start window. This is what makes it a form of brassage in the spectral dimension. The pattern in the weavfile then repeats, starting from the window it has now reached.

BLUR WEAVE can shorten or lengthen a sound: Shorten: suppose 3 windows are selected in a way which spans a total of 7 windows. For example, the weave pattern 3, -1, 5, starting from window 0 will take 3 steps, thus moving to window 3 (and selecting it for use in the outanalysisfile), move back one (3-1=2) and take window 2, and move forward 5 (2+5=7) and take window 7. Thus only 3 out of the 7 possible windows are written to the outfile, making the latter shorter by a ratio of 3:7. weavfile produces reduction by 0.43 new window count 0 1 2 3

(…see the CDP source for the full discussion.)

Musical applications

WEAVE can be used to shorten or extend a sound and/or to blur its characteristics: by taking windows out of sequence, earlier (backwards) or later (forwards) in the source. Windows taken from relatively distant locations of course mix up the sound quite a bit. A very different effect is achieved by having the windows hover around a certain area. The fact that the pattern repeats leads to additional possibilities to create pulsations in the sound, though the timbral effect is likely to vary due to changing spectral content as the weave moves through the source.

effects/bounce.title: bounce
effects/bounce.html:
bounce

Exposed effects: Bounce

Bounce

bounce.bounce · Extend & segment

Bounce the whole sound: accelerating repeats that die away, like a dropped ball settling.
  • Time-domain — operates directly on the audio.

Parameters

ParamMeaningRangeDefaultTime-varying
countBounces2 – 306—
startgapFirst gap (s)0.04 – 30.5—
shortenGap shrink0.4 – 10.8—
endlevelLast level0 – 10.1—
ewarpDecay warp0.5 – 31—

What it does

Bounce repeats the whole input sound count times, with the gaps between repeats shortening on each repeat, not unlike a bouncing ball. Startgap sets the initial delay time between repeats. Shorten sets the speed of the reduction (smaller is faster) and is a multiplier: for example, with Shorten = 1 the delay time is not reduced. To achieve the bouncing effect, each repetition is reduced in level: set endlevel and the sound reduces to this level over the course of count repeats. Ewarp bends the rate of decay: 1 a faster decay. If the optional min parameter is set, the repeated elements are themselves shortened in proportion to the accelerando; min sets a minimum length for the repeated elements. If no shrinkage is wanted, the parameter should be selected and set to zero. Finally, the "no overlap" flag (-c) ensures that elements will cut off at the next repetition to avoid clipping. (This can be a problem if the source is longer than startgap and the signal has multiple overlaps.)

effects/cascade.title: cascade
effects/cascade.html:
cascade

Exposed effects: Cascade echoes

Cascade echoes

cascade.cascade · Extend & segment

Echo successive segments of the source and superimpose the echo-sets.
  • Time-domain — operates directly on the audio.

Parameters

ParamMeaningRangeDefaultTime-varying
clipsizeClip (s)0.02 – 10.25—
echosEchoes1 – 648—
clipmaxClip max (s)0 – 20—
randRandomise0 – 10.3—

What it does

CASCADE echoes a given segment a number of times and mixes the echoes with the original soundfile (played 'straight'). There are five mode choices, all spatial, plus the ability to select the echo segment by size (clipsize) or from a list of cut-times (cuts), giving 10 modes overall. The segment size (Modes 1-5) is set by clipsize or randomly between this and clipmax. Similarly, the number of repetitions is set by echos or randomly between this and echomax. Shredno, shredcnt and the -a flag "shred original clip" offer possibilities to garble the segments and echoes.

Musical applications

The program is an alternative to EXTEND ITERATE, MODIFY REVECHO 3 (stadium echo), and MODIFY REVECHO 1/2 (delay line). CASCADE adds the unusual ability to select the segments and spatialise and/or shred the echoes.

clip

Hard-clip the waveform for distortion.

Exposed effects: Clip · Clip half-waves

Clip

clip.clip · Filter & dynamics

Hard-clip the signal at the given level (distortion).
  • Time-domain — operates directly on the audio.

Parameters

ParamMeaningRangeDefaultTime-varying
levelClip level0.01 – 10.3—

What it does

Clipping a signal cuts off the top of the waveform when the level exceeds 100%, introducing distortion. CLIP produces this distortion at lower signal levels. In Mode 1, level sets the level at which to clip the signal. This acts as a gate value: if too high, an error message may remind the user that the signal never reaches that level. If set lower, the signal is raised (or appears to be raised) so that all values that exceed that level are clipped. (In many cases, this may not result in an obvious distortion, because most of the signal may be unclipped.)

In Mode 2, half-waveforms are clipped at a given fraction of the original. This seems to give a more obvious distortion, even though the signal level appears to change little. Again, a lower value produces more clipping and more distortion.

Musical applications

...

effects/combine.title: combine
effects/combine.html:
combine

Combine the spectra of two analysis files.

Exposed effects: Spectral mean · Spectral cross · Spectral sum · Spectral difference · Spectral interleave · Spectral maximum

Spectral mean

combine.mean · Combine

Combine two sounds by taking the mean of their spectra (a hybrid).
  • Spectral — run through a pvoc anal → … → pvoc synth chain automatically; output is mono.
  • Two inputs — needs a second source.

Parameters

No parameters.

What it does

This program takes 2 input sounds and calculates the average of the 2 signals, spectral window by spectral window. The average in loudness between, for example, two speech sounds, should reach some vague mean between the formants of the speech components being used. The frequency average is altogether more strange. It may, for example, convert harmonic into inharmonic spectra. Seriously wierd.

Musical applications

It is not really possible to predict the results of this way to combine sounds, as they are so dependent on the nature of the sources. It is best to try it with the type of source file you favour and try to build up some experimental data about what happens.

Spectral cross

combine.cross · Combine

Replace the spectral amplitudes of the first sound with those of the second (cross-synthesis).
  • Spectral — run through a pvoc anal → … → pvoc synth chain automatically; output is mono.
  • Two inputs — needs a second source.

Parameters

ParamMeaningRangeDefaultTime-varying
interpAmount0 – 11yes

What it does

Understanding the ONEFORM COMBINE Function

This function takes information about the spectral contour (or formant-shape) of a sound at a specific time, extracted using ONEFORM GET, and combines it with pitch-trajectory information (a plot of changing pitch extracted using REPITCH GETPITCH) possibly derived from a different sound. The result will be a sound having the same pitch-trajectory, and using the 'colour' of the formant-shape.

Musical applications

This process may be used to create pitched, or pitch-changing events, using formant-shapes (e.g. vowel sounds from speech) extracted from a particular source. It is complementary to the processes which grab and extend FOFs, but works with (and outputs) analysis files, and operates in a different way.

ALSO SEE: COMBINE MAKE

Spectral sum

combine.sum · Combine

Add the two spectra together.
  • Spectral — run through a pvoc anal → … → pvoc synth chain automatically; output is mono.
  • Two inputs — needs a second source.

Parameters

ParamMeaningRangeDefaultTime-varying
crossoverMix in 2nd0 – 11yes

What it does

COMBINE SUM examines the amplitude levels in each channel of each of the two input analysis files. Where they differ, it adds this difference to the 1 st file, as weighted by crossover. In other words, the result is infile plus the difference between it and infile2. When resynthesising, watch out for clipping.

Musical applications

This is a way to adjust the timbre of a sound by adding to it some part of of the timbral features which belong to another sound. Very often, the change is both major and relatively unpredictable.

Also see: COMBINE DIFF.

Spectral difference

combine.diff · Combine

Subtract the second spectrum from the first (spectral cancellation).
  • Spectral — run through a pvoc anal → … → pvoc synth chain automatically; output is mono.
  • Two inputs — needs a second source.

Parameters

ParamMeaningRangeDefaultTime-varying
crossoverSubtract 2nd0 – 11yes

What it does

In COMBINE DIFF one spectrum is subtracted from another on a channel-by- channel basis (weighted by crossover). If amplitude in any channel goes negative, you can opt whether or not to retain the negative amplitudes.

By default, the setting of any amplitudes < 0 to 0 protects against negative overflow, but you can use the -a flag and see what happens.

Musical applications

This is a way to change a sound on a very experimental basis.

Also see: COMBINE SUM.

Spectral interleave

combine.interleave · Combine

Interleave alternating blocks of analysis frames from the two sounds.
  • Spectral — run through a pvoc anal → … → pvoc synth chain automatically; output is mono.
  • Two inputs — needs a second source.

Parameters

ParamMeaningRangeDefaultTime-varying
leafsizeLeaf (windows)1 – 644—

What it does

COMBINE INTERLEAVE interleaves N spectra from N analysis files, thereby constructing a new analysis file as output. The spectral characteristics of several sounds are thus amalgamated into one new sound.

The degree to which the original sounds are retained depends on the number of analysis windows used.

(…see the CDP source for the full discussion.)

Musical applications

With very small values for leafsize, the various sounds are mingled quite thoroughly and relatively smoothly - relative to the nature of the input sounds, though a somewhat grainy effect may result. With larger values for leafsize, say 8, 10, 20 or more, more of each component sound is heard in each leaf and the result is more like a churning or pulsating effect as the new soundfile oscillates among the sound material in the various source soundfiles. To churn means to shake, stir or agitate violently, as when making butter from milk, which is nicely descriptive of what happens when several sound sources, each fairly strong, are interleaved in this way. [It's one of my favourites! - A.E].

Spectral maximum

combine.max · Combine

Keep, in every channel and frame, the louder of the two spectra.
  • Spectral — run through a pvoc anal → … → pvoc synth chain automatically; output is mono.
  • Two inputs — needs a second source.

Parameters

No parameters.

What it does

COMBINE MAX studies the data in all the input analysis files. For each channel it retains only the single loudest spectral component among all the input files. In spite of the loss of the other components, the sound often remains the same to a remarkable degree. But how several sounds will merge in this way will be a little unpredictable: because data from the files which DO NOT have the loudest spectral component will simply be omitted.

The spectral characteristics of the input sounds are just merged, producing an ultra-seamless mix. The input sounds remain recognisable, just like an ordinary mix. Note that this is different from the programs which transfer the spectrum or spectral envelope of a sound. With the latter, the audible characteristics of one of the sounds are noticeably changed.

(…see the CDP source for the full discussion.)

effects/constrict.title: constrict
effects/constrict.html:
constrict

Shorten or close up the silent gaps within a sound.

Exposed effects: Tighten silences

Tighten silences

constrict.constrict · Extend & segment

Shorten (or close up) the silent gaps in a sound, tightening its rhythm.
  • Time-domain — operates directly on the audio.

Parameters

ParamMeaningRangeDefaultTime-varying
constrictionTighten by (%)0 – 200100—

What it does

This is a form of time-contraction which does not time-stretch the sonic-substance of the source. Note that the constriction is a percentage. Thus: 50 will halve the silent gaps 75 will take away three quarters of the silent gaps 20 will reduce them to one-fifth their original length 100 will eliminate the silences 150 will cause the non-silent portions to overlap by half the duration of the original silences

It works only with soundfiles which contain areas of zero-level signal which can be contracted by the process.

Musical applications

CONSTRICT can be used to take a sequence of rapidfile events separated by silences and make them even tighter.

effects/crumble.html:
crumble

Exposed effects: Crumble to 8 channels · Crumble to 16 channels

Crumble to 8 channels

crumble.crumble · Spatialisation

Project a mono sound onto an 8-channel ring, then progressively crumble it into segments scattered over smaller and smaller channel groups.
  • Time-domain — operates directly on the audio.

Parameters

ParamMeaningRangeDefaultTime-varying
startStart (s)0 – 50.1—
dur1Split-to-2 (s)0.2 – 80.35—
dur2Split-to-4 (s)0.2 – 80.35—
segsizeSegment size (s)0.02 – 10.1—
segrandSize randomness0 – 10.3—
pitchvarPitch variation (±st)0 – 122—

What it does

CRUMBLE projects mono segments over progressively smaller groups of channels in multi-channel space, with possible timestretch. Specifically, it projects the source onto all channels, then segments it and distribute the segments over smaller and smaller groups of channels.

The choice is limited to 8-channel or 16-channel output, but this can be reduced afterwards by PAIREX (extract stereo pairs) or CHANNELX (extract single chans) plus optional interleaving (INTERLX).
